summary:
Karachay-Cherkessia stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care have been banned outright since 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed. The Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises any public expression, explicitly including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and official national government warnings state this directly to LGBT travellers.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated movement or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night (The Guardian, 17 January 2024). Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 (The Moscow Times, 23 June 2025). In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility (Associated Press).

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) singles out the North Caucasus, including Karachay-Cherkessia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note records systematic regional campaigns from 2017 to 2024 that included abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and states that the 2023 extremist designation carries two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

North Caucasus SOS, whose coordinator David Isteev covers the North Caucasus republics including Karachay-Cherkessia, states that there is "no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus" and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. Isteev, an on-the-ground defender in exile, reports year-on-year deterioration across the republics he covers, and the organisation coordinates roughly 34 evacuations a year of people fleeing the region.
tangentialFactors:
The severity gradient runs against the national baseline rather than alongside it. The UK Home Office finds Russia non-persecutory in general while treating the North Caucasus as a distinct exception, which means a visitor's exposure in Karachay-Cherkessia is materially higher than the same visitor would face in most of the country.

The Chechnya precedent is the closest comparison: documented systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people from 2017 to 2024, including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and a pattern of forced return to families that North Caucasus SOS describes as routine across the republics.

National-level enforcement supplies the legal instrument for local action. The extremist designation introduced in 2023 converts possession or display of alleged symbols into an extremism charge carrying two to six years' imprisonment, and six to ten for organising, giving regional police a charge that applies regardless of local legislation.

Two foreign governments have issued explicit warnings bearing on entry and onward movement: the US State Department rates travel to Russia Level 4 with LGBT-directed advisories, and the UK Home Office note sets the standard by which Russian LGBT+ applicants are assessed for asylum.

The documented raid tempo after the Supreme Court ruling, and the eighteenfold growth in propaganda-law cases reported in June 2025, indicate that enforcement capacity is expanding nationally rather than contracting.
localsOnly:
Residents of Karachay-Cherkessia cannot obtain legal gender recognition: the 2023 law bars both gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents, and gender-affirming care is prohibited nationwide.

Residents face the same extremist-designation exposure as visitors, but with no exit option built in: charges under the administrative and criminal codes have produced 101 extremism-related convictions nationally as of 30 June 2025, and the propaganda statutes have generated more than 60 million rubles in fines over two years.

North Caucasus SOS operates an evacuation route for people leaving the region, coordinating roughly 34 evacuations a year, and David Isteev reports that conditions have worsened year on year across the republics he covers.

LGBT+ people from Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, are recognised by the UK Home Office as members of a particular social group under the refugee convention, which governs how UK asylum claims from the country are assessed.

Forced return to family is a named risk for residents as well as visitors: North Caucasus SOS records it alongside violence and detention as a consequence of even private existence in the region.
outOfScopeNotes:
No purge, raid or mass-violence incident specific to Karachay-Cherkessia is documented in the sources assembled here. The republic's risk assessment rests on the regional pattern described by the UK Home Office and North Caucasus SOS rather than on republic-level incidents, and republic-level enforcement figures remain unresolved.

Whether the eighteenfold growth in propaganda-law cases and the 101 extremism convictions recorded nationally include cases originating in Karachay-Cherkessia is not stated in the sources and is unresolved.

The conversion-therapy detention reported by BBC Russian took place near Novosibirsk, not in the North Caucasus; it evidences the national pattern of physical coercion against transgender people and is not sourced to this republic.

The date on which the UK Home Office country policy note was last page-updated is recorded inconsistently across sources and is unresolved; the note's stated version date is June 2025.

The current state of club raids, nightlife closures and public-space policing inside Karachay-Cherkessia itself is not sourced; the raid evidence cited here comes from Moscow.
